Problem 1

The given equation is

(1)Cdvdt=k(v−vr)(v−vt)−u+Idudt=b(v−vr)−u

Let v¯=V(v−vr),u¯=Uu, then

(2)dv¯dt=Vdvdtdu¯dt=Ududt

Plug it into the original equation, we have

(3)CVdv¯dt=kVv¯(v¯V+vr−vt)−u¯U+Idu¯dt=UbVv¯−u¯

Hence

(4)dv¯dt=kCv¯(v¯V+vr−vt)−VUCu¯+VICdu¯dt=UbVv¯−u¯

Let V=kC,U=kC2, α=k(vr−vt)C,β=bC,δ=kIC2, then the equations are transformed into

(5)dv¯dt=v¯2+αv¯−u¯+δdu¯dt=βv¯−u¯

which is desired. Note that V,U,β,δ are none-zero since C,I,vr,vt,k,b are non-zero. But α may be zero.

Problem 2

Set α=1 (and re-denote v¯ as v, u¯ as u), the system becomes

(6)dvdt=v2+v−u+δdudt=βv−u

(a) Rewrite the system into matrix form

(7)ddt[vu]=[v2+v−u+δβv−u]=[f1(v,u)f2(v,u)]=F(v,u)

At the critical points, we have

(8)ddt[vu]=0,{v2+v−u+δ=0βv−u=0⇒{v=12(β−1−s),u=β2(β−1−s)v=12(β−1+s),u=β2(β−1+s)

where s2=(1−β)2−4δ,s>0 and can take any non-negative value if fix β and vary δ. For convenience, let m0=(β−1)24.

The Jacobi matrix at (u,v) is

(9)J(v,u)=∇F(v,u)=[∂f1∂v∂f1∂u∂f2∂v∂f2∂u]=[2v+1−1β−1]

which contains no u. Fix v, we can find the eigenvalues of it at (v,u)

(10)|J(v,u)−λI|=|2v+1−λ−1β−1−λ|=0⇒{λ1=v−tλ2=v+t

where t2=(v+1)2−β.

Therefore,

  1. If (1−β)2<4δ, then s2<0, (8) has no solutions. I.e. there's no critical point.

  2. If (1−β)2=4δ, then s=0,v=β−12,t=12|b−1|4+b2, (8) has only one solution (critical point)

    (11)(v,u)=(β−12,β(β−1)2)

    at this critical point, since t2⩾0, the 2 eigenvalues are all reals.

    (12)λ1=12(β2−β−|β−1|β2+4),λ2=λ1=12(β2−β+|β−1|β2+4)

    Note that

    (13)dλ1dβ=(b−1)(−2b2+b−4)2(b−1)2(b2+4)+b−12,dλ2dβ=(b−1)(b(2b−1)+4)2(b−1)2(b2+4)+b−12

    We know that when β<1, dλ1dβ>0,dλ2dβ<0, and when β>1, dλ1dβ<0,dλ2dβ>0, the two functions are all piecewise. When β=1, λ1=λ2=0, hence on R, λ1⩽0 while λ2⩾0, equality hold iff β=1,δ=0. Therefore

    • If β=1, then δ=0, λ1=λ2=0, the critical point (11) is an unstable saddle point.

    • Otherwise, λ1<0,λ2>0, the critical point (11) is an unstable saddle point.

  3. If (1−β)2>4δ, then s2>0, s has 2 values, denoted −s,s without mess, one positive and one negative, (8) has 2 distinct solutions (critical points)

    (14)P1=(v1,u1)=[12(−β2−2β−4δ+1+β−1),12β(−β2−2β−4δ+1+β−1)]P2=(v2,u2)=[12(β2−2β−4δ+1+β−1),12β(β2−2β−4δ+1+β−1)]

    P1, P2 corresponds to −s,s respectively. Consider P2 first.

    At P2 t2=s+14(−1+b+s)2⩾0, hence λ1,λ2 are all real numbers. furtherly,

    (15)v2−t=12(s+β−1)−14(s+β−1)2+s⩽0

    Equality hold iff. s=0, i.e. β=1,δ=0. While

    (16)v2+t=12(s+β−1)+14(s+β−1)2+s⩾0

    Also equality hold iff. s=0, i.e. β=1,δ=0. Therefore as long as β≠1 or δ≠0, we have λ1<0,λ2>0, indicating that P2 is an unstable saddle point.

    At P1 If t2=14(s+1−β)2−s<0, solve t2<0, we have

    (17)β>0∧δ∈[−β3+2β2+β−2β,β3+2β2+β−2β]=[m1,m2]

    Denote this region as Rtn1 (blue).

    Solve v1>0,v2>0, we have

    (18)v1>0⇒β∈(1,+∞),δ∈(0,14(1−β)2](denoted as Rvp)

    • In Rvp∩Rtn, λ1, λ2 at P1 is imaginary and conjugated, v1>0 (orange), Re λ1,Re λ2>0, P1 is an unstable spiral

      Figure: unstable spiral and unstable saddle

    • Similarly, on Rvpc∩Rtn, λ1, λ2 at P1 is imaginary and conjugated, v1<0, it's a stable spiral.

      Figure: stable spiral and unstable saddle

    If t2=14(s+1−β)2−s>0, then λ1,λ2 are all real numbers. Note that if t>0, we have

    (19)14(1−β+s)2−s>0⇒β<0∨s∈(−∞,(1−β)2)∪((1+β)2,+∞)

    hence when β<1, (β,δ)∉Rtn,

    (20)λ1=v1−t<λ2=v1+t=−1−β+s2−−s+14(1−β+s)2<0

    λ1,λ2 are real and negative. Hence P1 is a stable sink.

    when β>1, (β,δ)∉Rtn,

    (21)λ2=v1+t<λ1=v1−t=−1−β+s2−−s+14(1−β+s)2>0

    λ1,λ2 are real and positive. Hence P1 is a unstable source.

    Boundary Now we dive into the boundary occasions.

    ∂Rtn∩Rvpc On the yellow boundary, t=0 while v1<0, hence R∋λ1,λ2<0 at P1, P1 is a degenerated stable sink.

    ∂Rvp∩Rtn On the green boundary, t2<0 while v1=0, hence λ1,λ2 are conjugated pure imaginary numbers, P1 is a center.

    ∂Rtn∩Rvp On the blue boundary, t=0 and v1>0, hence R∋λ1,λ2>0, P1 is a degenerated unstable source.

    β=1,δ=0 There is a special point β=1,δ=0 to discuss. When taking this parameter, the critical point is (0,0), the Jacobi matrix is

    (22)J(v,u)=[2v+1−11−1]=[1−11−1]

    of which the eigenvalues are 0. Thus we should take second order derivative:

    (23)H(v,u)=[2000]

    Hence it is a saddle point.

    Now we have discussed all behaviors when (β,δ) is varying.

(b) Set β=2, the equation becomes

(24)ddt[vu]=[v2+v−u+δ2v−u]=[f1(v,u)f2(v,u)]=F(v,u)

If furtherly δ=0, referring to the debate in (a), since (1−β)2>4δ, there're 2 critical points P1=(0,0),P2=(2,1), and at P1, λ1=λ2=0, P1 is a center.

Besides, when β=2, we get s2=1−4δ, t2=−1 at P1 and t2=2 at P2. Referring to the debate above in (a), m0=14 and in (17), m1=−4−32,m2=−4+32

  • when δ<−4−32, there're a stable sink and an unstable saddle.

  • when −4−32<δ<0, there're a stable spiral and an unstable saddle.

  • when δ=0, there're a center and an unstable saddle point.

  • when −4+32>δ>0, there're an unstable spiral and a saddle.

  • when δ=−4+32, there're an degenerated unstable source and a saddle.

  • when 14>δ>−4+32, there're an unstable source and a saddle.

By (8),

(25)P1=(u1,v1)=(12(1−1−4δ),1−1−4δ)P2=(u2,v2)=(12(1+1−4δ),1+1−4δ)

as δ increases, u1↑, u2↓, u2>u1, v1↑, v2↓, v2>v1,

We can conclude that there's a homoclinic bifurcation when δ goes through.

(c) If there is limit cycles, then there could be some δ,β, making the eigenvalues of the Jacobi at the center of the trajectory purely imaginary (sufficient condition). Thus, by the discussion above, we must have v=0 and t2=(1+v)2−β<0. To make critical point exist, we must have β>0.

Since v=12(−(β−1)2−4δ+β−1)=0, we have β⩾1,δ=0.

  • Assume β=1,δ=0, by the debate above, P2 is a stable center, hence there exists infinite limit cycles around it.

  • When β≠1, as

    (26)∂f1∂v+∂f2∂u=2v≠0,∀ (u,v)∈R2

    Applying Bendixson's Criterion, the system has no closed trajectories inside R−×R∪R+×R.

  • According to the index theory, there must be a sink, source or center when a closed orbit presents.

    In summary, we can conclude that limit cycles exist if β>1 and δ=0.

    The following graph shows the existence of a limit cycle when β=3, δ=0:

(d) To produce homoclinic orbits, we'd better produce saddle point first. By (c), when β>1,δ=0, there appears a center P1 and a saddle point P2, note that the trajectory emitted from P2, hence there exists homoclinic orbits for the same parameter values.

(e) The bifurcation occurs when 14(1−β)2=δ, and at this time, the critical point

(27)v=12(β−1),u=β2(β−1)

Hence the parametric expression of the curve of the points where bifurcation occurs should be

(30)Cv(β)=(14(1−β)2,β−12),Cu(β)=(14(1−β)2,β(β−1)2)

If we put it onto the vu plane, then the expression is

(31)C(β)=(β−12,β(β−1)2)

When β<1, P2 is stable, otherwise, it's unstable.

Question 3

I chose 2 sets of parameters which produce distinct behaviors:

one is the only parameter region in which a stable center appears. i.e. β>1,δ=0. The corresponding phase plane, by the debate above, contains a saddle point in the first quadrant, coordinates at (β−1,β(β−1)), and a center, coordinated at (0,0), they're symmetric about the origin. See the animation below:

At β=1, the 2 critical point will merge to a single one, and the limit cycles (closed trajectories) will disappear. As β exceed 1, those critical point will disappear as well. Near the saddle, we can calculate out the eigenvectors of its linearized expression. For example, when β=2, the saddle is (1,2) the Jacobi matrix is

(32)J(1,2)=[2β−1−12−1]=[3−12−1],λ1=1+2,v1=(1+2,2)T,λ2=1−2,v2=(2−1,2)T

Hence along the line (1,2)+μ(1+2,2), the trajectories will converge to (1,2) but along the line (1,2)+μ(−1+2,2), the trajectories will diverge.

Also, at the other critical point (center) (0,0), the Jacobi matrix is

(33)J(0,0)=[1−12−1],λ1=i,v1=(1+i,2)T,λ2=−i,v2=(1−i,2)T

Hence the trajectories around (0,0) is counter-clockwise.

This behavior indicates that when k or I is nearly zero (membrane capacitance), if we set b>C and a non-zero small recovery current, they will oscillate of the nearly same range of amplitude and reaching steady state costs a long time.

The other is the region that no stable critical point exists. i.e β>1,δ>0. When the membrane potential |v| is large enough, we can find that u′/v′ is small, hence the change of recovery current will be small, thus the trajectories will be more horizontal.

At this time, there're at most 2 (or 1 or none) unstable critical points, one is unstable saddle, the other is an unstable source or unstable spiral. For example, when β=3,δ=0.1, The critical point in the first quadrate is (6,2) and the Jacobi matrix is

(34)J(1,2)=[1.1026−12−1],λ1≈0.05+0.95i,v1≈(0.43+0.39i,0.82)T,λ2≈0.05−0.95i,v2≈(0.43−0.39i,0.82)T

Thus the spiral is contour-clockwise and unstable. Nearly all trajectories will diverge to the far right.

This behavior indicates that when b>C (membrane capacitance) and δ>0, any initial membrane potential and recovery current will result in the destruct of the cell neutron (surely exactly on the critical point will prevent this, but any small perturbation will result in this). The steady-state of the neutron cannot be recovered anymore.
